Naples on foot

The must-sees

  • Capodimonte

    Museum

    Charles of Bourbon built it to hold the Farnese art collection he inherited from his mother. Caravaggio’s Flagellation of Christ hangs here.

    Look for: Find Queen Maria Amalia’s porcelain parlour, a small room with walls covered entirely in porcelain, moved here from the royal palace at Portici.

  • Cappella Sansevero

    Museum

    Giuseppe Sanmartino carved the Veiled Christ in 1753, making a thin shroud seem to lie over the body. The chapel belonged to Raimondo di Sangro, Prince of Sansevero, an alchemist and inventor.

    Look for: Francesco Queirolo’s Disillusion shows a man struggling free of a fishing net, every knot cut in marble.

  • Castel Nuovo

    Fortress

    Charles I of Anjou built it in the late 13th century, and Neapolitans still call it the Maschio Angioino. The Aragonese rebuilt it and added the triumphal arch celebrating Alfonso V’s entry into the city in 1443.

    Look for: In the marble arch between the towers, a relief shows Alfonso’s triumphal procession, the king seated high on his chariot.

  • Castel dell’Ovo

    Fortress

    The islet of Megaride is where Greek settlers first landed. Legend says the poet Virgil hid a magic egg in the foundations, and that if it breaks the city will fall.

    Look for: At the foot of the castle, the little harbour of Borgo Marinari is crowded with fishing boats and restaurant tables.

  • Naples Cathedral

    Church

    Several times a year the dried blood of San Gennaro, the city’s patron saint, is shown to the faithful, who watch for it to liquefy. The Royal Chapel of the Treasure holds the saint’s relics and a rich collection of gifts.

    Look for: Off the left aisle, the early Christian basilica of Santa Restituta survives inside the cathedral, with a baptistery said to be the oldest in the West.

  • National Archaeological Museum

    Museum

    Its collections include the Farnese marbles and the Alexander Mosaic from Pompeii. The building started life in the 16th century as a cavalry barracks and then housed the university.

    Look for: On the ground floor, walk round the giant Farnese Hercules leaning on his club: he hides the golden apples of the Hesperides behind his back.

  • Piazza del Plebiscito

    Square

    It is named after the 1860 vote that joined Naples to the Kingdom of Italy. Once a car park, it was cleared of traffic in the 1990s and is now used for concerts and gatherings.

    Look for: Facing the palace, the church of San Francesco di Paola copies Rome’s Pantheon, its dome rising behind the curving colonnade.

  • Royal Palace of Naples

    Palace

    Built for the Spanish viceroys in the early 17th century, it later housed the Bourbon kings. The niches on the facade hold statues of rulers of Naples, added in the 19th century.

    Look for: The eight kings on the facade run in order of dynasty, from Roger the Norman to Victor Emmanuel II. Napoleon’s brother-in-law, Joachim Murat, stands among them.

  • Spaccanapoli

    Neighbourhood

    It follows the line of a street of the Greek city of Neapolis. From the hill of San Martino it looks like a single cut through the rooftops, which gave it its name.

    Look for: At the western end, the church of Gesù Nuovo has a facade of pyramid-shaped stones, left from the palace it was before the Jesuits rebuilt it.

  • Teatro di San Carlo

    Venue · 1737

    Opened in 1737 by Charles of Bourbon, it is the oldest opera house in Europe still in use. It burned in 1816 and was rebuilt within a year.

    Look for: Inside, the royal box sits at the centre of the horseshoe of boxes, topped by a large gilded crown.

  • Via Caracciolo

    Waterfront

    Closed to traffic, the promenade is busy with walkers, runners and swimmers on the rocks. Vesuvius and Capri frame the view across the bay.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Naples and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Naples passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
